To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the best exploration algorithms lacking any knowledge of a graph use twice as many edge crossings in the worst case than do the best exploration algorithms that have an unoriented graph map.

the best exploration algorithms lacking any knowledge of a graph or a tree use twice as many edge crossings in the worst case than do the best exploration algorithms having a complete knowledge about the graph or the tree.

the best graph exploration algorithms lacking knowledge of the graph use more edge traversals in worst case than do the algorithms with unoriented maps of the graph, which in turn use more edge traversal than the best algorithms with complete knowledge of the graphs.

the problem of graph exploration, which is the problem of traversing a connected undirected graph in order to explore its vertices and edges.
the problem of finding the best exploration algorithms for undirected connected graphs.
the problem of exploring an unknown graph.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the best exploration strategy without knowledge of the topology of the environment is twice as bad as the best exploration strategy with knowledge of the topology, but without the ability to orient the map, and that the best strategy with knowledge of topology and the ability to orient is twice as good as the best strategy without knowledge of topology.
the more knowledge the algorithm has about the graph to be explored, the more efficient it can be.
the topographic information is of crucial importance in graph exploration, and the more the better.

the more information the robot has about the graph, the better the performance of the exploration algorithm is.
